Mixture-of-experts (MoE) routing collapse is the failure mode where the router — a learned linear or softmax layer that assigns tokens to experts — stops distributing load and instead funnels most or all tokens to a small subset of experts, leaving the rest undertrained and useless. The central question here is whether this collapse is deterministic given an architecture and dataset, or whether it's a phase transition whose onset location in training depends sensitively on how the router weights are initialized — and crucially, how that sensitivity changes when you vary the expert capacity factor (the hard cap on how many tokens each expert can process per batch). The capacity factor is the lever practitioners use to enforce load balancing: if an expert is full, excess tokens are dropped or passed through a residual, which means routing decisions have asymmetric consequences that feed back into gradient signals differently depending on whether you're in a capacity-constrained or capacity-slack regime. What a beginner misses is that initialization variance doesn't just affect early training dynamics uniformly — it interacts with the capacity constraint to create bifurcated gradient landscapes: under tight capacity, high initialization variance can prevent collapse early by forcing diversity (tokens spill over and train multiple experts), while under loose capacity, that same variance accelerates collapse by letting early random routing imbalances compound without corrective pressure. The expert worry is therefore not "does initialization matter" (it obviously does) but rather whether there exist initialization variance thresholds that are stable in one capacity regime and catastrophically unstable in another, because this would mean that a hyperparameter that looks safe during development at generous capacity can cause silent collapse when capacity is tightened for inference efficiency.

The key property is gradient flow through dropped tokens. When an expert is at capacity, tokens routed to it but rejected receive no gradient from that expert's computation — their router logits get a signal only from the auxiliary load-balancing loss (e.g., the importance loss in the original GShard paper, or the load loss in Switch Transformer), not from the task loss. This means that below the capacity boundary, every routing decision is connected to task-loss gradients and initialization variance translates into diverse but informative gradient directions that push experts toward specialization. Above the capacity boundary — where many tokens are dropped — a large fraction of router updates come only from the auxiliary loss, which pushes toward uniform distribution regardless of what the task actually rewards, effectively decoupling router learning from expert quality. The flip happens because high initialization variance in the capacity-slack regime creates early routing diversity that generates rich, task-coupled gradient signal across all experts, but in the capacity-constrained regime that same variance means more tokens are dropped earlier, starving the task-loss gradient path and leaving the auxiliary loss dominant — which in Switch Transformer (Fedus et al., 2021) used a coefficient as small as 1e-2 precisely because it was known to overwhelm task gradients if unchecked. Lepikhin et al. (GShard, 2021) observed that with capacity factor 1.0, routing decisions for overflow tokens essentially became detached from downstream quality, and subsequent work on Expert Choice routing (Zhou et al., 2022) reframed the whole problem by letting experts select tokens rather than vice versa, specifically to eliminate this gradient detachment asymmetry. The practical implication is that initialization variance controls how quickly you saturate capacity in the first forward passes, and once saturation is widespread, you've already committed to a gradient regime that auxiliary losses alone may not be strong enough to escape.

There are principled proposals, but the honest answer is they mostly mask rather than close the problem. The most direct approach is to treat the auxiliary loss coefficient as a control variable in a feedback loop: measure per-expert capacity utilization each step, compute deviation from target (e.g., 1/num_experts), and adjust the coefficient via something like a PI controller — this is essentially what DeepSeek-V2 (2024) does with their "dynamic auxiliary loss scaling," reporting that fixed coefficients caused oscillation between collapse and over-regularization while adaptive scaling stabilized utilization near target without dominating task gradients. However, this is still operating on the symptom (uneven utilization) rather than the cause (gradient detachment from dropped tokens), because no matter how well you balance load, tokens that get dropped still receive no task-loss gradient for that routing decision — the feedback loop just ensures fewer tokens are dropped on average, reducing but not eliminating the detachment. A more structurally honest fix is to eliminate hard dropping entirely: ST-MoE (Zoph et al., 2022) experimented with router z-loss as a replacement regularizer that penalizes large router logits directly, which discourages confident early routing without any capacity-gating mechanism, and found it more stable than auxiliary load loss at equivalent compute — but it changes what the router learns to do, biasing toward lower-confidence routing that may hurt expert specialization. The deepest issue is that dynamic coefficient adjustment is a scalar acting on a vector problem: it can shift the mean gradient contribution from the auxiliary loss but cannot selectively restore task-loss gradients to the specific token-expert pairs that were dropped, so the information about which expert would have been better for those tokens is simply gone. Closing the problem fully requires either never dropping tokens (which has memory cost proportional to num_experts × sequence_length), or computing a surrogate gradient for dropped tokens — something like a straight-through estimator through the capacity gate — which to date remains largely unexplored in published MoE work at scale.

A straight-through estimator (STE) through the capacity gate would pass gradients as if the gate were always open — meaning the router receives task-loss signal for dropped tokens as if they had been processed, which creates a systematic lie: the router is told "your routing decision was consequential" when the token actually contributed zero to the forward pass. The most predictable degeneracy is confidence amplification toward already-popular experts: the router learns to route dropped tokens even more aggressively to the full expert, because the STE gradient says that expert was good for those tokens (based on whatever that expert computed for the tokens it did accept), reinforcing the exact imbalance that caused dropping in the first place — a positive feedback loop that is structurally identical to the rich-get-richer dynamic Shazeer et al. (2017) originally identified in the noisy top-k gating paper and tried to break with explicit noise injection. A subtler degeneracy is phantom specialization: experts appear to specialize on token types they never actually process at full capacity, because their logged routing statistics reflect intended assignments rather than actual computations, making diagnosis extremely difficult — your utilization metrics look balanced while your experts are learning from a corrupted signal. Compared to collapse, this degeneracy is arguably worse in one specific sense: collapse is visible (you can measure expert utilization and see 90% of tokens going to two experts), whereas STE-induced phantom specialization can produce superficially healthy utilization statistics while the router's learned behavior is nonsensical, making it a silent failure mode. The closest published analogy is the behavior observed when people apply STE through top-k selection in sparse attention (Correia et al., 2019 on sparse transformers) — they found that STE through discrete selection gates caused the model to learn overly confident selections that were brittle to distribution shift, precisely because gradients flowed through paths that weren't actually taken. The degeneracy is recoverable in principle if you weight the STE gradient by the token's drop probability (a kind of importance-weighted correction), but this requires estimating that probability per-token per-step, adding overhead that likely negates the efficiency motivation for capping capacity in the first place.

The honest reading of the evidence is that well-functioning MoE routing is closer to a managed saddle point than a stable basin, and the practical literature inadvertently confirms this through what it requires to maintain good routing: auxiliary losses, capacity constraints, router z-loss, periodic load monitoring, and sometimes manual intervention — a constellation of continuous corrective forces that would be unnecessary if the well-behaved solution were genuinely attracting. The strongest direct evidence comes from the ST-MoE ablations (Zoph et al., 2022), where removing the router z-loss mid-training caused rapid routing degradation even in models that had been stable for tens of thousands of steps, implying the good solution had no restoring force of its own and was being actively held in place. DeepSeek-MoE (2024) provides complementary evidence: their architectural choice to use many fine-grained experts (64 experts, top-8 routing) with shared "always-on" experts was explicitly motivated by the observation that routing stability required the loss landscape to be less sensitive to any single routing decision — they were effectively widening the saddle by reducing the consequence of individual router errors, not finding a deeper basin. The most theoretically careful analysis is in Lewis et al. (2021) on BASE layers, which reframes routing as a linear assignment problem and shows that the task-loss gradient with respect to router parameters is nearly flat in the well-balanced region — meaning the router has weak incentive to stay balanced from the task loss alone, which is precisely the geometry of a saddle rather than a minimum. Against this, the Expert Choice paper (Zhou et al., 2022) is the strongest argument for a genuine basin: by inverting the routing direction, they eliminate the capacity gate entirely and report stable training without auxiliary losses on several benchmarks — but critics note this changes the problem by removing token agency, and it's unclear whether the stability reflects a true attractor or just a less volatile saddle. The practical implication is severe: if good routing is a saddle, then initialization variance doesn't just affect whether you reach good routing but how long you can maintain it before perturbations (batch composition shifts, learning rate changes, domain shifts) knock you off — and no published work has systematically measured this residence time as a function of initialization.

Router architecture does change saddle curvature, and the mechanism is the rank and smoothness of the routing function's input-output map. A linear probe (the standard: a weight matrix W of shape d_model × num_experts followed by softmax) produces routing decisions that are globally smooth but low-rank — the router can only distinguish tokens along num_experts directions in the full d_model-dimensional space, which means perturbations in the orthogonal complement cause zero routing change, effectively flattening the saddle in most directions and making the router insensitive to many input perturbations but also unable to recover from them. A small MLP router increases effective rank by composing nonlinearities, giving the router more expressive routing boundaries, but this cuts both ways: higher curvature around the saddle means stronger restoring forces when perturbed slightly, but also steeper descent paths toward collapse attractors — empirically, Mixtral's routing (Jiang et al., 2024) uses a linear router and the authors explicitly note they found MLP routers unstable in early experiments, consistent with the steeper-descent interpretation. Dot-product attention over learned expert embeddings (as in CoE, Mixture of Experts with Learned Routing, and variants) introduces a fundamentally different geometry: the routing decision depends on the relative position of token representations and expert embedding vectors in a shared space, which means the saddle's curvature is coupled to expert embedding updates — if experts drift during training, the routing landscape deforms continuously, creating a non-stationary saddle that is harder to maintain but potentially self-correcting if expert embeddings and token representations co-adapt. The most concrete curvature measurement in the literature comes from Zoph et al.'s router z-loss analysis, which shows that linear routers develop very large logit magnitudes over training (sometimes exceeding 20-30 in absolute value), indicating the softmax is operating in a near-saturated regime where gradients are vanishingly small — the saddle has effectively become a near-cliff, highly stable locally but with catastrophic drop-off if crossed. The underexplored insight is that router architecture determines not just expressivity but the Hessian structure at the saddle, and a linear router's low-rank Hessian may actually be preferable in practice not despite but because of its insensitivity — it limits both the rate of collapse and the rate of recovery, trading dynamism for robustness in a way that MLP and attention routers do not.

The key diagnostic is not utilization but the intrinsic dimensionality of the joint token-expert embedding space over time. Stabilizing co-adaptation looks like token representations and expert embeddings spreading into distinct, well-separated clusters in that shared space — measurable via the effective rank of the cross-attention matrix between token representations and expert embeddings, which should plateau or slowly increase; slow-moving collapse looks like that effective rank decreasing while utilization metrics remain flat, because tokens and experts are drifting into alignment along a shrinking subspace before the routing distribution visibly tips. The most actionable early warning signal is the singular value spectrum of the router's attention matrix: in stabilizing co-adaptation you expect a relatively flat spectrum (many singular values contributing), while pre-collapse shows a spectrum where the top-1 or top-2 singular values begin absorbing disproportionate variance — this is detectable hundreds or thousands of steps before utilization entropy drops, analogous to how the singular value spectrum of weight matrices was used as a training health diagnostic in the spectral analysis of Transformer training by Biderman et al. (2023) on Pythia models. Anthropic's interpretability work on superposition provides a complementary framing: if expert embeddings are being pushed into superposition with token representations (multiple token types mapping onto the same expert direction), effective rank metrics will show false stability while the routing function is actually becoming degenerate — you'd need to measure not just rank but the coherence between expert embedding vectors, where increasing cosine similarity between expert embeddings is a leading indicator of collapse even when utilization looks uniform. The practical obstacle is that these diagnostics require logging the full embedding matrices at regular checkpoints and computing SVD at model scale, which for large MoE models (DeepSeek-V2 has 160B parameters across 160 experts) is non-trivial — most production training pipelines log only scalar utilization statistics precisely because tensor-level diagnostics are expensive, which is why slow-moving collapse goes undetected. The irreversibility threshold appears to be crossed when expert embeddings have collapsed to near-identical vectors, because at that point the attention router has lost the geometric diversity needed to produce differential routing signals regardless of what the token representations do — and no amount of auxiliary loss adjustment can restore diversity in the expert embedding space without an explicit repulsion term, which to date appears in no major published MoE system.

Geometric repulsion between expert embeddings is implementable — the natural form is a pairwise cosine similarity penalty added to the training loss, something like λ · Σᵢⱼ max(0, cos(eᵢ, eⱼ) - margin), which penalizes expert embeddings eᵢ, eⱼ for becoming more similar than a target margin — and the dead neuron revival analogy is apt but reveals the core tension immediately: in sparse autoencoders (Anthropic's work on dictionary learning, 2023-2024), dead feature revival works by reinitializing dead neurons to high-loss input directions, which is safe because features haven't developed task-relevant structure yet; expert embeddings by contrast encode routing geometry that the rest of the network has already adapted to, so repulsion doesn't just separate embeddings, it actively moves the targets that token representations are trying to hit. The destructive interaction is most likely when repulsion is applied to embeddings that are similar because they genuinely serve similar token populations — if two experts have converged to handle punctuation and short function words respectively, their embeddings may be legitimately close in the shared space, and forcing separation will route those token types to experts that haven't developed the right feed-forward structure for them, causing a temporary but potentially severe task loss spike. The most relevant empirical precedent is from continual learning rather than MoE: elastic weight consolidation (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017) showed that geometric constraints on parameters that encode task-relevant structure cause catastrophic interference proportional to the Fisher information at those parameters — the analogy for expert embeddings is that repulsion applied along directions of high routing sensitivity (high Fisher information with respect to the routing loss) will be destructive, while repulsion along low-sensitivity directions is essentially free, suggesting a Fisher-weighted repulsion that only pushes embeddings apart in directions the router isn't currently using. DeepSeek-V3's auxiliary-loss-free routing (2024) hints at a softer version of this intuition: they use a bias term per expert that is updated based on load, effectively nudging routing without touching embedding geometry directly — this avoids destructive interference but also can't recover from true embedding collapse since it operates downstream of the attention computation. The timing of repulsion injection matters as much as its form: applied before collapse (as a preventive term from initialization), repulsion has no task-relevant structure to destroy and straightforwardly maintains diversity — this is the regime where it would work cleanly, analogous to how orthogonal initialization (Saxe et al., 2014) prevents rank collapse in linear networks without interfering with learning because it's applied before any structure exists. The open question is whether there's a detectable transition point — perhaps the singular value threshold mentioned in the previous turn — at which repulsion switches from safe to destructive, which would make it a viable intervention if monitored carefully but a liability if applied as a static regularizer throughout training.
